lines: Following [NATS ADR-37](https://github.com/nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design/blob/fac1b7e7ff96498afbb768b11d3d313f10c14ff3/adr/ADR-37.md#buffering-messages), Swoole refills at the buffer's half-full watermark. Handing a message to a handler frees buffer space immediately; acknowledgement frees in-flight capacity separately. One receive is outstanding at a time. Its size is the buffer's free space, clamped by available in-flight capacity. All limits must be positive. A tight in-flight limit applies backpressure even if the buffer has room; slow acknowledgements cannot accumulate unbounded deliveries. NATS uses `Consumer\Streaming` and the client’s `fetchEach()` to hand off each arrival before the pull finishes. This lets handlers and renewals progress even when the shared broker window is full. Redis and other array-based consumers retain batched delivery. Renewals cover all held messages, including buffered work. Buffered jobs can start during a slow receive; shutdown returns unstarted work and drains running jobs before closing the consumer.

-**Queue 7 receive-buffer migration:** `prefetch` previously meant the total unacknowledged limit. Set `maxInFlight` explicitly to that old value to retain the old reservation budget, and choose receive-buffer capacity separately. The new default reserves room for both handlers and a buffer, so the total allowance doubles when `prefetch` is omitted. Review NATS `maxAckPending` across all replicas; it is shared broker flow control, not the per-worker receive buffer. Exclusive consumers require `maxInFlight: 1`. Third-party adapters overriding `run()` must accept the new optional `maxInFlight` argument. NATS requires client 1.7 or newer for incremental pulls; publish that before queue 7 and the Platform update. Pooled consumers retain their existing serialized batch path; use a dedicated NATS consumer with a connection factory for incremental delivery and concurrent commands.

Consumers retain `receive(Queue $queue, int $timeout, int $n = 1): array`, `commit()`, and `reject()`. Sparse queues return available messages without waiting to fill a batch. Each message has an independent outcome. Completed requests already waiting on a connection are coalesced without a timer; handlers can continue while confirmations are pending, within the same delivery bound. Success hooks run after their own confirmation, so a later handler can start before an earlier success hook.

Third-party consumers keep the existing `Consumer` contract. `commit()` acknowledges processed work; `reject()` applies the broker's retry/dead-letter policy. Optional `release()` returns work whose handler never started. On Redis it never counts as an attempt. A NATS NAK always counts toward `maxDeliver`, so `Broker\Nats` instead requeues the message as a new one, which starts with no attempts, and acknowledges the original once the copy is stored. The requeued job joins the back of the queue. Only a successful requeue is free. On a bounded work stream with `DiscardPolicy::Old`, where a requeue would evict the oldest stored job, or when the requeue is refused, it falls back to a NAK after `releaseDelay` seconds (default 5), which spends an attempt. If the connection fails before the NAK reaches the server, the original is redelivered after `ackWait`, which also spends one. If the copy is stored but the ack is lost, the job is delivered twice. Existing single-message `extend()` implementations remain supported alongside variadic renewal; no new renewal interface is required. Receipt identity stays opaque on `Message` and is separate from its message ID.

The NATS client’s `fetchEach()` delivers arrivals incrementally. Queue consumers built with a connection factory can process and acknowledge them while the pull is pending; shared live connections retain serialized batch delivery.

`Connection::requestBatch()` sends typed requests together using the same lifecycle as `request()`. `JetStream::ackBatch()` translates selected messages into individual acknowledgement requests and owns their confirmation semantics. Successful results are delivered before unrelated replies time out. Ambiguous writes are not replayed. The queue coalesces acknowledgements already waiting on its command connection, retaining per-message confirmation and error handling. If that connection disconnects, a broker configured with a connection factory drops its cached connection and handles under the lock. The next operation opens a new connection without replaying the failed operation or dropping other in-flight deliveries.
